items.title: Banner Years: 1961, Celtics achieve elite status with third straight championship
items.content:
(Photo by UPI/Bettmann Archive/Getty Images) | Getty Images NBA history spans 80 seasons, and as CelticsBlog readers well know, the Boston Celtics have won a league-high 18 championships. This month, we are recapping each of those title years. Elite Three-Peat The Boston Celtics reached an elite milestone by winning the NBA Finals in 1961, adding to their 1959 and 1960 banners. They became just the second franchise to collect a trio of consecutive titles. The first was the Minneapolis Lakers from 1952 to 1954. Since then, the Chicago Bulls won three straight championships from 1991 to 1993, and a second time, 1996 to 1998, and the Los Angeles Lakers won from 2000 to 2002. No team has won more than three straight years except the Celtics, who went for eight in a row. as we know.

Bill Russell received many MVP trophies in his career. Here’s one with congratulations from NBA president Maurice Podoloff. (Photo by Bettmann Archive/Getty Images)

The MVP A large factor in Boston’s success, literally, was 6-foot-10 center Bill Russell, who in five seasons changed the Celtics from a pretty good team to a dynasty with four titles. Russell was awarded Most Valuable Player of the 1960-61 season in a vote by players, which was the process then. Oddly, Russell was chosen to only second team All-NBA, behind Wilt Chamberlain, but that vote was by sportswriters. (Insert pondering-face emoji.) This was Russell’s second MVP (1957-58 was the first). He would win five in his career because of his defense, rebounding, passing and intellect. To this day, he is universally known as the best defensive player of all time. In fact, as calculated by basketball-reference.com, he has the highest Regular Season Defensive Win Share, the highest Playoff DWS and the highest Total DWS of anyone who’s ever played in the NBA or ABA. By far. Unfortunately, the Defensive Player of the Year award was created more than a decade after Russell retired. The regular season In 1960-61, NBA conventional wisdom was that the Celtics had gotten too good for the rest of the league. The results supported that theory, as both the regular season and postseason were nearly drama-free for the two-time defending champs. The season began with an adjusted schedule, going from 75 games per team to 79. The Celtics’ final record was 57-22, which was 11 games ahead of the Eastern second-place Philadelphia Warriors and six games better than the West-leading St. Louis Hawks. Boston was third in scoring at 119.4 points per game while allowing a league-low 114.1. The Celtics also easily won the season series against all of the other teams, the only one close being St. Louis (6-4). The blueprint to success The rest of the league had to be wondering when they would ever beat Boston again. But as the saying goes, there were levels to this, and head coach and general manager Red Auerbach knew it. items.title: The NBA’s 7 worst offseason moves of 2026, ranked
items.content:

(Photo by G Fiume/Getty Images) | Getty Images	The best thing about the parity era of the NBA is that almost every team believes they are one or two moves away from contention. It can also be something of a double-edged sword when teams get desperate and make shortsighted deals that could negatively affect their chances for years to come if they don’t go right.

It’s always hard to tell which bold decisions are going to pay off. I was a big fan of the New York Knicks trading for Karl-Anthony Towns, but a lot of outlets thought his huge contract and poor defense made him a toxic asset. The Knicks ended up looking like geniuses for the KAT trade during their 2026 championship run. I also liked the Phoenix Suns’ trade for Kevin Durant a couple years ago, and that one ended up being a massive whiff on my part.

Big risks can equal big rewards in the NBA, but some of the decisions this summer already seem destined to age poorly. Here’s my list of the worst moves of the NBA offseason thus far.

7. Lakers break the bank for Walker KesslerOf all the moves on this list, this one has the chance to come back and bite me. I’m pretty high on the Lakers entering the season. Luka Doncic and Austin Reaves needed a defensive-minded center behind them, and Kessler was the best one available on the market. I don’t even really have a problem with Kessler’s contract, a four-year, $130 million deal, which seems fine for a solid starting center. My issue is what the Lakers gave up to get him, sending two unprotected first-round picks and two swaps to Utah for the right to pay him. That’s a superstar haul for a player who has never come close to being an All-Star before, and I doubt he’ll ever achieve that status. The deal also means the Lakers don’t have a first-round pick to trade for the next seven years. Los Angeles might have the worst forward room in the league at the moment, and they have no way to upgrade the roster after overpaying for Kessler. This could work out if Luka looks like the best player in the world and Kessler looks like prime Rudy Gobert, but it’s just way too risky for a player who has accomplished very little in his NBA career thus far.

6. Knicks letting Mitchell Robinson walkI understand that no team wants to be in the second apron right now, but I think it could have been worth it for the Knicks to re-sign Mitchell Robinson.
